meaning: Logging in with two or more different kinds of proof, such as a password plus a code.
Logging in with exactly two different kinds of proof, such as a password and your phone.
An encrypted tunnel that carries your traffic over a network you don’t control.
Flooding a service with traffic from many machines at once so real users can’t reach it.
Any attack that knocks a service offline or makes it unusable.
The encrypted version of the web protocol, shown by the padlock in your browser.
A web address. Checking the real domain in it is a key phishing defence.
The rules for addressing and routing data between devices on a network.
The company that connects your home or office to the internet.
A short numeric secret used to unlock a card, phone or account.
A code that works for a single login, then expires.
Standard text messaging. Phishing by text is called smishing.
The law that sets how organisations must collect, use and protect personal data.
Any data that can identify a person, such as a name, address or National Insurance number.
The core software that runs a device, such as Windows, iOS or Android. Keep it updated.
The standard plug for drives and devices. Unknown USB sticks can carry malware.
The security standard that encrypts Wi-Fi. WPA3 is the current version.
The internet’s phone book, turning names like example.com into IP addresses.
Letting staff use their personal phones and laptops for work.
One login that gives you access to many apps.
Everyday connected devices like cameras, doorbells and smart plugs, often poorly secured.
A network covering one home, office or building.
A network linking sites across large distances, such as offices in different cities.
The UK’s technical authority for cyber security, part of GCHQ.
The UK regulator for data protection. Serious personal data breaches are reported to it.
The three core goals of security: keep data secret, accurate and accessible.
Very short-range wireless, used for contactless payments and tapping to pair.
Apps you use in the browser while the provider runs everything, like Microsoft 365.
A defined way for software to talk to other software. Exposed APIs are a common target.
An old way to move files that sends everything, including passwords, unencrypted.
The senior leader responsible for an organisation’s security.
A contract promising to keep shared information confidential.
Only the sender and recipient can read messages, not even the service in between.
The square barcode. Phishing with fake QR codes is called quishing.

meaning: The puzzle a site shows to check you’re a person, not a bot.
The name of a Wi-Fi network. Attackers copy it to set up fake hotspots.
Tools that let IT enforce settings on, and wipe, work phones and tablets.
Security software on laptops and servers that spots suspicious behaviour and can isolate the device.
An outsourced team that watches your alerts around the clock and responds to threats.
A system that collects logs from everywhere and correlates them to spot attacks.
The team that monitors for and responds to security incidents.
A DNS record listing which servers are allowed to send email for a domain.
The public catalogue that gives each known vulnerability an ID, like CVE-2021-44228.
Managing who people are and what they’re allowed to access.
Giving access by job role rather than person by person.
A filter in front of a website that blocks attacks like SQL injection.
Watches network traffic and raises alerts on signs of attack, without blocking.
Like an IDS, but it actively blocks the malicious traffic it spots.
Lets many devices share one public IP address, as your home router does.
The encryption behind HTTPS and secure email. It replaced SSL.
The older, now broken predecessor of TLS. People still say ‘SSL certificate’.
The system of certificates and authorities that proves who owns which encryption keys.
The standard symmetric cipher used to encrypt most data today.
A skilled, well-funded attacker, often state-backed, who stays hidden in a network for a long time.
Injecting malicious script into a web page so it runs in other users’ browsers.
A flaw that lets an attacker run their own code on your system from afar. The worst kind.
An attacker secretly relays, reads or changes traffic between two parties.
Information gathered from public sources, like social media, often used to tailor phishing.
How the organisation keeps running during a disruption.
How IT systems and data are restored after a major incident.
Publishes standards such as ISO 27001 for information security.

decoys: National Institute of Security and Technology
National Institute for Standards and Testing
National Institute of Software and Technology
meaning: The US body behind the widely used Cybersecurity Framework.
The person who oversees an organisation’s data protection compliance.
Tools that stop sensitive data leaving, for example by blocking emails with card numbers.
A person’s legal request to see the personal data an organisation holds about them.
When a product stops getting security updates and should be replaced.
The chip that ties a phone to your number. SIM swapping hijacks texted login codes.
Renting servers, storage and networks from a cloud provider. You secure what you build on them.
A cloud platform to build and run apps without managing the servers underneath.
Lets an app access your account without your password. Fake consent requests abuse it.
Windows remote control. Exposed to the internet, it’s a favourite way in for ransomware.
An encrypted way to log in to and manage remote systems from the command line.
The protocol that sends email between servers. On its own it doesn’t check who the sender is.
Servers around the world that serve a site’s content quickly and absorb DDoS traffic.
Evidence of an attack, such as a known bad IP address or file hash.
The servers attackers use to send instructions to infected machines.
Gangs rent out their ransomware to affiliates for a cut of the ransom.
A separate network segment for public-facing servers, kept apart from the internal network.
Systems that control physical equipment, such as factory lines and power grids.
An outside firm that runs your IT. Attackers target them to reach all their customers.
One component whose failure brings everything down.
A battery unit that keeps equipment running through a power cut.
The original Wi-Fi encryption. It can be cracked in minutes, so never use it.
Analysed information about attackers and their methods, used to prepare defences.
The last part of a domain, like .com or .co.uk. Phishers swap it to make lookalikes.
Fraud using a hijacked or spoofed business email account, often to redirect payments.
Phone calls over the internet. Caller ID is easy to fake, which helps vishing.
An attacker gains control of a real user’s account, often with stolen passwords.
A list of rules saying who or what can access a resource.
Detection and response that joins up endpoints, email, network and cloud in one view.
Tools that automate routine incident steps through playbooks.
Sits between users and cloud apps to enforce security policy and spot risky use.

decoys: Domain-based Message Authorisation, Reporting and Conformance
Domain-based Mail Authentication, Reporting and Compliance
Domain-based Message Authentication, Routing and Conformance
meaning: Tells receiving servers what to do with email that fails SPF and DKIM checks.
A digital signature on email that proves it came from the domain and wasn’t altered.
Scores a vulnerability’s severity from 0 to 10 to help prioritise patching.
A list of every component inside a piece of software, so you can tell if a flaw affects you.
How a particular attacker behaves, as mapped in MITRE ATT&CK.
Locking down, checking out and recording the use of admin accounts.
Grants access app by app after checking user and device each time, replacing the old VPN model.
Networking and security delivered together from the cloud, close to the user.
Tricks a logged-in user’s browser into sending a request they didn’t mean to make.
Works out which activities matter most and how long each can be down.
The longest a system can be down before the impact is unacceptable.
The most data you can afford to lose, measured in time since the last backup.
The policies and processes for managing security risk, as defined in ISO 27001.
A required check of privacy risks before starting high-risk processing of personal data.

decoys: Payment Card Industry Data Safety Standard
Payment Card International Data Security Standard
Payment Card Industry Digital Security Standard
meaning: The security rules for any organisation that stores, processes or sends card data.
A tamper-resistant device that generates and guards encryption keys.
A security chip in a computer that stores keys and checks the device boots safely.
The modern firmware that starts a computer, replacing the BIOS. It enables Secure Boot.
Encrypts a whole drive, so a lost laptop doesn’t leak its data. BitLocker is one example.
A standard that passes login details between an identity provider and apps for single sign-on.
The standards behind passkeys and security keys, which resist phishing.
The protocol apps use to look up users and groups in a directory like Active Directory.
Hands out IP addresses to devices automatically when they join a network.
Maps IP addresses to hardware addresses on a local network. ARP spoofing enables man-in-the-middle attacks.
How networks on the internet announce routes to each other. Hijacking it can reroute traffic.
On average, how long it takes to notice an incident. Lower is better.
The team that handles security incidents from first alert to lessons learned.
Learns normal behaviour for users and devices, then flags unusual activity.
Give people and systems only the access they need, and nothing more.
Prove who you are, control what you can do, and record what you did.
Systems that run industrial processes, from water treatment to manufacturing.
Software that monitors and controls industrial equipment across sites, such as a power grid.
The six-digit code in an authenticator app that changes every 30 seconds.
Scans source code for security flaws without running it.
Tests a running app from the outside, the way an attacker would.
Continuously checks cloud accounts for misconfigurations, such as storage left public.
Phishing that relays your login through a proxy to steal the session, even with MFA.
UK rules on marketing emails, texts, calls and cookies.
Reads email while keeping it on the server, so every device sees the same mailbox.
Downloads email to one client and usually removes it from the server.
Software that moves email between mail servers, like a sorting office.
Recipients hidden from everyone else on the email; used to hide mass phishing.
Outlook in a web browser; its sign-in page is often faked in phishing.
A domain with non-Latin characters; can be abused for lookalike addresses.
The protocol web browsers use to request and receive web pages.
The markup that structures web pages and styled emails, including links.
Malware that gives an attacker remote control of a victim’s computer.
An older hashing algorithm with known collision weaknesses.
The current standard for file hashing, producing a 256-bit fingerprint.
Microsoft rules that block risky behaviour, like Office apps creating executables.
The SIEM side for real-time monitoring, correlation and alerting.
Detects and responds to threats using network traffic and telemetry.
The binary file format modern Windows event logs are stored in.
The query language used to search logs in Azure Monitor and Log Analytics.
Splunk’s query language, chaining commands together with pipes.
The language for querying databases; osquery uses it to query endpoints.
Captured network traffic saved for later analysis in tools like Wireshark.
Used to monitor and manage network devices like routers and switches.
A standard for exporting network flow records, based on NetFlow.
Syslog value worked out as facility × 8 + severity.
A structured text format often used by cloud APIs to deliver log data.
A style of web API that cloud services use to expose data over HTTP.
Published internet standards, such as RFC 5424 for Syslog.
